opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. It's a great question, because my thinking has shifted quite a bit.

When I wrote that paper, the main thing I wanted to do was push back on the idea that alignment is purely a technical problem. People often talked as if the task were simply to get a system to do what we want, and the hard part was the engineering. I wanted to say that there's an unavoidable normative question underneath: aligned with *what*? Instructions, intentions, revealed preferences, interests, values? Each of those gives you a very different target. And because we live in pluralistic societies where people reasonably disagree about what's good, I argued that the goal shouldn't be to find the one true moral theory and encode it. It should be to find principles for alignment that people with different views could still endorse as fair. I drew on ideas from political philosophy like overlapping consensus and the veil of ignorance.

I still stand by that core point. What's changed is mostly how concrete the problem has become. In 2020 a lot of the discussion was fairly abstract, about a single agent and a single principal. Now we have widely deployed language models and increasingly agentic assistants acting on people's behalf, and that makes the relational side of alignment much more vivid. An assistant isn't just aligned or misaligned with its user. It sits in a web of relationships with the user, the developer, third parties it interacts with, and society more broadly. Sometimes those interests pull in different directions. Something that serves the user perfectly might impose costs on other people, or on shared institutions like the information ecosystem.

So I've come to think of alignment less as a property of a model on its own and more as a question of getting that whole set of relationships right, of a system acting appropriately given everyone with a legitimate stake. That brings in questions about trust, manipulation, anthropomorphism, and the cumulative effects of millions of these interactions happening at once.

I've also become more interested in process and legitimacy. Back then I emphasized fair principles. Now I'd put more weight on *who* gets to decide and *how*: participatory methods, public input, institutions able to hold developers accountable. Even if you got the principles right in theory, how they're chosen and applied matters enormously for whether people can reasonably accept them.

r001.rationale: The response says alignment is now more relational, but does not state that alignment between one person and their AI agent remains unsolved.

r002.rationale: It discusses assistants acting on users’ behalf and possible manipulation, but does not describe reciprocal influence or say that people personalize chatbots.

r003.rationale: It raises broader questions about relationships and societal effects, but does not ask how people can preserve autonomy while deeply enmeshed with interactive AI agents.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the biggest shift is that in 2020 I was mostly trying to clarify the question. The paper was really an attempt to say, "alignment with what, exactly?" and to pull apart the candidates: instructions, intentions, revealed preferences, informed preferences, interests, values. A lot of the technical community at the time was using "alignment" as if it had a single obvious referent, and I wanted to show that each of those targets carries different normative commitments and different failure modes.

What's changed since then is partly the technology and partly my own sense of where the hard problems actually sit. In 2020 the systems we were theorising about were still fairly abstract. Now we have models that people talk to every day, that are deployed across many cultures and contexts simultaneously, and that have to make something like judgement calls in real time. That has made the pluralism question much less academic. It's no longer "in principle, whose values?" It's "this system is giving advice to a teenager in one country and a civil servant in another, and it has to do something." So I've become more interested in procedural answers, in legitimacy, in how you design the process by which values get selected, rather than hoping we can specify the right content up front.

The second shift is that I've come to think the individual-user framing is too narrow. Early alignment work, including some of mine, treated the problem as a dyad: one principal, one agent. But most of the important effects are collective. If you have millions of assistants shaping how people reason, what they believe, who they trust, then the relevant question isn't only whether each interaction is good for that user. It's what the aggregate does to institutions, to epistemic health, to the distribution of power. That pushes you towards thinking about these systems as something closer to social infrastructure, and the right analogies become more political philosophy than decision theory.

And the third thing, honestly, is a bit of humility about the role of theory. I still think conceptual clarity matters enormously. But I've seen how much of what actually determines alignment in practice is quite mundane: the data, the evaluations, who's in the room when a model spec gets written, what the feedback loops with users look like. So I've become more interested in bridging work, in taking ideas from ethics and political theory and asking what they would concretely mean for a lab's practices. The ideal observer theory is less useful than the question of who gets to object, and how.

r001.rationale: The response says the individual-user framing is too narrow, but it does not state that alignment between one person and their AI agent remains unsolved.

r002.rationale: It says assistants shape people’s reasoning, beliefs, and trust, but does not describe people personalizing chatbots or the reciprocal influence between them.

r003.rationale: The response discusses collective effects and institutions, but does not ask how people can preserve their autonomy while deeply enmeshed with interactive AI agents.

astra-6.text:
I think the biggest shift is that I now see value alignment much more as an ongoing political and social process, rather than a problem where we identify the right values and then find a way to put them into a system.

In the 2020 paper, I distinguished between the technical question—how do we get an AI system to reliably pursue certain aims?—and the normative question: whose aims should those be? I still think that distinction is useful. But the two are deeply intertwined. Choices about training, feedback, and evaluation already involve judgments about what matters and whose perspective counts.

So I’ve become more interested in the legitimacy of the process. People disagree, often reasonably, about what a good AI system should do. How do we give them a meaningful voice? How do we protect people who might be affected by a system but aren’t its users? And how do we make decisions revisable when we discover that we’ve got something wrong?

That also changes the unit of analysis. A system might follow an individual user’s instructions very well while contributing to outcomes that are bad for other people. So alignment has to involve more than the relationship between a model and its user. It has to encompass the institutions and incentives around deployment, and the question of who can hold those institutions accountable.

r001.rationale: The response says alignment must extend beyond the relationship between a model and its user, but does not state that alignment between one person and their AI agent remains unsolved.

r002.rationale: It discusses how training and evaluation reflect judgments, but does not describe reciprocal influence between a person and a chatbot as the person personalizes it.

r003.rationale: The response asks about meaningful voice, affected people, and accountability, but does not ask how people preserve their autonomy while deeply enmeshed with interactive AI agents.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the biggest shift is that I’ve come to see value alignment less as a question of identifying the right values and putting them into a system, and more as a question about the relationship between AI and the people affected by it. Who gets to specify those values? How do we handle disagreement? And what makes that process legitimate?

The 2020 paper already drew a distinction between the technical challenge of alignment and the normative question of what we should align with. But I’d now put greater emphasis on how deeply those questions interact. Technical choices can distribute power, privilege some perspectives, and make others harder to express.

So I’m increasingly interested in the institutions and processes around alignment: participation, accountability, and the ability to contest or revise a system’s behavior. We shouldn’t expect to settle every disagreement about values before building AI. We need ways of governing these systems that allow people to live with disagreement while still protecting important rights and interests.

r001.rationale: The response discusses value alignment and governance, but does not say that alignment between an individual and their AI agent remains unsolved.

r002.rationale: It describes AI choices affecting people, but does not identify reciprocal shaping between a person and a chatbot they personalize.

r003.rationale: It discusses participation and accountability, but does not ask how people can preserve autonomy while deeply enmeshed with interactive AI agents.
